description: Deterministic frozen evaluation corpus for SPPU engineering RAG retrieval evaluation.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: A Linker is a system program that combines one or more object modules generated by compilers or assemblers into a single executable binary image. It performs address resolution and symbol relocation. A Loader is responsible for loading the executable binary image from secondary storage into primary RAM memory and initiating its execution. Types of loaders include absolute loaders, relocating loaders, direct linking loaders, and dynamic link loaders.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Relocation in loaders refers to the process of modifying memory addresses in object code so that the program can execute correctly from any starting address allocated by the operating system. Relocation bits or relocation dictionaries specify which machine instructions or address constants must be adjusted relative to the load origin.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: A Macro is a single unit of source code statement that expands into a sequence of assembly language instructions. The Macro Processor uses databases such as Macro Name Table (MNT), Macro Definition Table (MDT), and Argument List Array (ALA). In Pass 1, macro definitions are processed, MNT and MDT entries are populated. In Pass 2, macro calls are expanded by replacing formal parameters with actual arguments.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Differences between Macros and Subroutines / Functions: A macro expands in-line at each point of invocation during pre-processing or assembly, which increases executable code size but eliminates function call overhead. A subroutine maintains a single copy of code in memory, using call and return instructions with stack frame manipulation, saving memory at the cost of execution time overhead.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Phases of a Compiler: Lexical Analysis (scanning tokens), Syntax Analysis (parsing parse tree / AST), Semantic Analysis (type checking), Intermediate Code Generation (three-address code), Code Optimization, and Target Code Generation. The symbol table stores identifiers, types, scopes, and memory offsets across all phases.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Lexical Analyzer (Scanner) groups source code characters into meaningful sequences called lexemes and produces tokens. It removes whitespace and comments. Tools like LEX use regular expressions to generate finite state automata for token recognition.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Top-Down Parsing versus Bottom-Up Parsing: Top-down parsers (such as recursive descent and LL(1) parsers) construct parse trees starting from the root start symbol down to the leaves using leftmost derivations. Bottom-up parsers (such as Shift-Reduce, LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1)) reduce tokens toward the start symbol using rightmost derivations in reverse.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Process Control Block (PCB) contains process state (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated), process ID (PID), program counter, CPU registers, CPU scheduling information (priority), memory management information (page tables), and I/O status information. A context switch saves the state of the active process into its PCB and restores another process state from its PCB.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: CPU Scheduling Algorithms: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) suffers from the convoy effect; Shortest Job First (SJF) is optimal for minimizing average waiting time but can cause starvation; Round Robin (RR) uses a fixed time quantum for preemptive time-sharing systems; Priority Scheduling executes highest priority processes first, using aging to prevent indefinite starvation.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanisms enable processes to exchange data and synchronize. Common IPC mechanisms include shared memory, message queues, pipes (anonymous pipes and named pipes / FIFOs), and sockets. Shared memory provides fastest communication without kernel intervention after setup, while message passing uses send() and receive() system calls.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Critical Section Problem and Synchronization: A critical section is a code segment accessing shared resources. Any solution must satisfy three requirements: Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting. Synchronization primitives include Mutex locks and Semaphores. Counting semaphores control access to a finite set of resources; binary semaphores behave like mutexes using wait() and signal() operations.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Deadlock Characterization: A deadlock situation occurs if and only if all four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. Deadlock prevention invalidates at least one of these conditions, while deadlock avoidance uses algorithms like Banker's Algorithm.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance: Utilizes data structures Available vector, Max matrix, Allocation matrix, and Need matrix (Need = Max - Allocation). The safety algorithm tests whether the system is in a safe state by iteratively finding a process whose resource request can be satisfied with currently available resources plus reclaimed allocated resources.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Paging is a memory management scheme that eliminates external fragmentation by partitioning physical memory into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates logical addresses (page number and page offset) into physical addresses (frame number and frame offset) using a page table. Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) acts as a hardware cache for page table entries.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Page Replacement Algorithms: When a page fault occurs and no free frame is available, a page replacement algorithm selects a victim page. FIFO replaces the oldest page and may suffer from Belady's Anomaly. Optimal (OPT) replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period in the future (used as a theoretical benchmark). Least Recently Used (LRU) replaces the page that has not been referenced for the longest time.

chunks.subject: SPOS
chunks.content: Disk Scheduling Algorithms optimize the movement of the disk read/write head to minimize seek time. Algorithms include FCFS, Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF), SCAN (Elevator algorithm), C-SCAN (Circular SCAN), LOOK, and C-LOOK. SSTF selects the request with minimum seek distance from the current head position, but can cause starvation for distant requests.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: OSI 7-Layer Reference Model vs TCP/IP Model: The OSI layers from bottom to top are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. In TCP/IP, Session and Presentation are merged into Application. The Physical layer transmits raw bits; Data Link handles framing and MAC addressing; Network handles logical IP addressing and packet routing; Transport ensures end-to-end communication via TCP or UDP.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: Network Topologies: Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh, and Hybrid topologies. In Star topology, all devices connect to a central hub or switch; failure of one cable does not bring down the entire network, though central switch failure causes outage. Mesh topology connects each node to every other node, providing redundancy and fault tolerance at higher cabling cost.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: Error Detection and Correction: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) treats data bitstrings as polynomials and divides by a predefined generator polynomial. The remainder is appended as checksum. Hamming Code provides single-bit error correction and double-bit error detection by placing parity bits at powers of 2.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: Sliding Window Protocols: Stop-and-Wait ARQ has sender window size 1 and low link utilization. Go-Back-N (GBN) allows sender window N with cumulative ACKs; when a frame is damaged, all subsequent frames are retransmitted. Selective Repeat (SR) maintains receiver window > 1 and selectively retransmits only damaged frames, requiring independent ACK per frame.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: IPv4 Addressing and Subnetting: Classful addressing divides 32-bit addresses into Class A, B, C, D (multicast), and E (reserved). CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) uses subnet masks (e.g. /24) to allocate variable-length blocks. Subnetting splits a network into smaller sub-networks, reducing broadcast domain size and conserving IP addresses.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: Routing Algorithms: Distance Vector Routing (Bellman-Ford algorithm) exchanges routing tables with immediate neighbors and suffers from the Count-to-Infinity problem, mitigated by split horizon and poison reverse. Link State Routing (Dijkstra's Shortest Path algorithm used in OSPF) floods link state packets to all nodes, building a complete global topology map.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: TCP vs UDP: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is connection-oriented, reliable, stream-based, provides flow control (sliding window) and congestion control (Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, Fast Retransmit, Fast Recovery), established via 3-Way Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is connectionless, unreliable, message-oriented, with minimal header overhead suitable for real-time audio/video streaming and DNS.

chunks.subject: CN
chunks.content: Application Layer Protocols: Domain Name System (DNS) maps human-readable domain names to IP addresses using UDP port 53. HTTP/HTTPS operates over TCP port 80/443 for web documents. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, and default gateways to client hosts using DORA process (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge).

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: Database Management System (DBMS) architecture: Three-Schema Architecture consists of Physical/Internal Level (how data is physically stored), Conceptual/Logical Level (entities, data types, relationships, constraints), and External/View Level (individual user views). It provides logical and physical data independence.

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling: Core components include Entities (strong and weak entities), Attributes (simple, composite, multi-valued, derived, key), and Relationships (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many). Extended ER (EER) adds Specialization, Generalization, and Aggregation.

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: Relational Algebra Operations: Fundamental unary operations include Selection (sigma) and Projection (pi). Binary operations include Cartesian Product (cross), Union (cup), Set Difference (-), and Rename (rho). Derived operations include Natural Join, Theta Join, Outer Joins (left, right, full), and Division.

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: Database Normalization eliminates redundancy and update/insert/delete anomalies. 1NF requires atomic attribute values. 2NF removes partial functional dependencies on candidate keys. 3NF removes transitive dependencies (X -> A where X is superkey or A is prime attribute). BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) requires that for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: ACID Properties of Transactions: Atomicity (all operations execute or none do, ensured by recovery manager), Consistency (preserves database integrity constraints), Isolation (concurrent transactions execute without interfering, ensured by concurrency control), and Durability (committed changes persist even during system crashes, ensured by write-ahead logging).

chunks.subject: DBMS
chunks.content: Concurrency Control Techniques: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol requires a Growing Phase (acquiring locks) and a Shrinking Phase (releasing locks). Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until transaction commit to prevent cascading aborts. Timestamp Ordering protocol orders transactions based on system timestamps, aborting conflicting younger/older transactions.

chunks.subject: TOC
chunks.content: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) and Non-deterministic Finite Automata (NFA): A DFA is defined as a 5-tuple (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) where the transition function delta maps Q x Sigma to Q deterministically. An NFA maps Q x Sigma (or epsilon) to 2^Q (power set of states). Every NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA using Subset Construction.

chunks.subject: TOC
chunks.content: Moore and Mealy Machines: Finite state machines with output capabilities. A Moore machine produces output associated strictly with its states: lambda maps Q to Delta. A Mealy machine produces output associated with state transitions: lambda maps Q x Sigma to Delta. Mealy machines generally require fewer states than equivalent Moore machines.

chunks.subject: TOC
chunks.content: Regular Expressions and Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages: Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, Kleene star, intersection, and complementation. The Pumping Lemma states that any sufficiently long string w in a regular language (|w| >= p) can be split into w = xyz satisfying |y| > 0, |xy| <= p, and xy^i z is in the language for all i >= 0. It is used to prove that a language is not regular.

chunks.subject: TOC
chunks.content: Context-Free Grammars (CFG) and Pushdown Automata (PDA): A CFG is defined as G = (V, T, P, S). Normal forms include Chomsky Normal Form (CNF where productions are A -> BC or A -> a) and Greibach Normal Form (GNF). A Pushdown Automaton (PDA) augments a finite automaton with a stack (LIFO) storage, recognizing context-free languages.

chunks.subject: TOC
chunks.content: Turing Machines (TM) and Decidability: A Turing Machine is a 7-tuple (Q, Sigma, Gamma, delta, q0, B, F) featuring an infinite tape and a read/write head that moves left or right. It accepts recursively enumerable languages. The Halting Problem, which asks whether an arbitrary TM will halt on a given input, is undecidable as proven by Alan Turing using diagonalization.
